Dhaka hosted Test cricket before Bangladesh even existed.
On 1 January 1955, Pakistan played India at the Dacca Stadium, now the Bangabandhu National Stadium.
Bangladesh won its first ever One Day International against Kenya in 1998.
It happened in Hyderabad, India, with spinner Mohammad Rafique starring with bat and ball.
At its very first World Cup, in 1999, Bangladesh beat Pakistan.
The win at Northampton in England came against one of the tournament's finalists, and it helped Bangladesh gain Test status.
Bangladesh's first Test win came against Zimbabwe in January 2005.
It was played in Chattogram, more than four years after Bangladesh's first Test.
Bangladesh still holds the record for the youngest Test centurion.
Mohammad Ashraful scored a hundred against Sri Lanka in 2001 when he was 17 years and 61 days old.
Bangladesh's women won the 2018 Asia Cup.
They beat India in the final in Kuala Lumpur with a last-ball win.
Bangladesh won the Under-19 Cricket World Cup in 2020.
The final in South Africa was against India. It was Bangladesh's first world title in cricket.
Bangladesh's women footballers won the South Asian championship twice in a row.
They lifted the SAFF Women's Championship in 2022 and 2024, both times beating hosts Nepal in Kathmandu.
The men's football team won the SAFF Championship in 2003.
Bangladesh won the final at home in Dhaka on a penalty shoot-out against the Maldives.
Niaz Murshed of Bangladesh was the first grandmaster in South Asia.
He earned chess's highest title in 1987, before anyone from India.
Bangladesh has not yet won an Olympic medal.
It has sent athletes to every Summer Games since 1984, mostly in shooting, archery, swimming and athletics.
Brojen Das from Bangladesh swam the English Channel in 1958.
He was the first person from Asia to swim it, and crossed it several more times after that.
Bangladesh co-hosted the 2011 Cricket World Cup, and the opening ceremony was in Dhaka.
It was held at the Bangabandhu National Stadium, with India and Sri Lanka as the other hosts.
The 1930 World Cup final used two different footballs.
Argentina and Uruguay could not agree on a ball, so each team's ball was used for one half. Uruguay won with theirs in the second half.
The fastest goal in World Cup history came after 11 seconds.
Hakan Şükür scored it for Turkey against South Korea in 2002.
The World Cup trophy was once stolen and found by a dog.
The old Jules Rimet trophy disappeared in London in 1966. A dog named Pickles sniffed it out under a hedge a week later.
The football World Cup trophy is solid 18-carat gold.
It weighs about 6 kg. The winners keep only a gold-plated copy; FIFA keeps the real one.
Yellow and red cards were inspired by traffic lights.
Referee Ken Aston thought of the idea while waiting at a junction in London. They were first used at the 1970 World Cup.
The penalty kick was invented by a goalkeeper.
William McCrum, an Irish keeper, suggested it, and football's rule makers added it in 1891.
One Test match in 1939 was stopped after ten days with no winner.
The 'Timeless Test' in Durban had no time limit, but England had to catch their ship home, so the game was left as a draw.
A cricket pitch is 22 yards long because of an old way of measuring land.
That length is one 'chain', a unit surveyors used in England for centuries.
The word 'hat-trick' comes from cricket.
In 1858, bowler H. H. Stephenson took three wickets in three balls, and fans collected money to buy him a hat.
The Ashes are named after a joke death notice.
After Australia beat England at home in 1882, a newspaper wrote that English cricket had died and 'the body will be cremated'. A small urn of ashes became the prize.
Cricket bats have a width limit because of one cheeky batsman in 1771.
Thomas White walked out with a bat as wide as the stumps. A rule soon limited bat width.
The 2019 Cricket World Cup final was decided by counting boundaries.
England and New Zealand tied the match and then the super over. England won on most boundaries, a rule that was later changed.
The rain rule in cricket is named after two statisticians.
Frank Duckworth and Tony Lewis created it in the 1990s. It is now called DLS, after Steven Stern improved it.
The fastest ball in cricket was recorded at 161.3 km per hour.
Shoaib Akhtar of Pakistan bowled it against England at the 2003 World Cup.
Olympic gold medals are mostly made of silver.
Rules say they must be at least 92.5 percent silver, covered with at least 6 grams of gold.
Each Olympic ring colour was chosen so every nation's flag had at least one.
Pierre de Coubertin designed the rings in 1913. Blue, yellow, black, green and red on white covered all flags of the time.
Volleyball was first called Mintonette.
William Morgan invented it in 1895 in the USA as a gentler game than basketball for older players.
Badminton is named after a house in England.
The Duke of Beaufort's home, Badminton House, is where the game became popular in the 1800s.
A badminton shuttlecock can fly faster than 500 km per hour.
That makes it the fastest object in any racket sport, though it slows down very quickly because of its feathers.
Table tennis balls were made bigger in 2000 to slow the game down.
They grew from 38 mm to 40 mm so rallies would be longer and easier to follow on TV.
A golf ball has about 300 to 500 small dents for a reason.
The dimples make air flow hug the ball, cutting drag so it flies roughly twice as far as a smooth ball.
A hawk keeps pigeons away at Wimbledon.
A Harris hawk named Rufus has flown over the courts for years to scare off birds before play.
In theory, a Formula 1 car could drive upside down on a ceiling.
At high speed its wings push it down with more force than its own weight.
A marathon has been run in under two hours, but it doesn't count as a record.
Eliud Kipchoge ran 1:59:40 in 2019 with rotating pacers and other help that official races don't allow.
At his fastest, Usain Bolt ran about 44 km per hour.
During his 9.58-second world record in 2009, his peak speed was about 44.7 km per hour.
There are more possible games of chess than atoms in the observable universe.
Claude Shannon estimated about 10 to the power 120 possible games, while the universe has roughly 10 to the power 80 atoms.
India has won eight Olympic gold medals in field hockey.
That is more than any other country. Six of them came in a row from 1928 to 1956.
The first Women's Football World Cup was held in 1991, in China.
The USA won it. Twelve teams took part.
Video assistant referees were first used at a men's World Cup in 2018.
VAR helped referees check goals, penalties and red cards at the tournament in Russia.
Basketball's first nets had no hole at the bottom.
Early games used closed baskets, so someone had to fetch the ball after every score. Open nets came in the early 1900s.
Sepak takraw is like volleyball, but you cannot use your hands.
Players in South-East Asia kick, knee and head a rattan ball over a net, often with stunning bicycle kicks.
The Tour de France covers about 3,500 km in three weeks.
Riders can burn around 5,000 to 8,000 calories on a tough mountain day.
Swimming pools at the Olympics are kept at a set temperature.
The water must be between 25 and 28 °C, so muscles stay warm but swimmers do not overheat.
In tennis, 'love' means zero, but no one is sure why.
One popular idea says it comes from the French 'l'oeuf', meaning the egg, because a zero looks like an egg.
Kabaddi players must keep saying 'kabaddi' in one breath while raiding.
If the raider stops chanting before getting back to their half, they are out.
The longest tennis match took more than 11 hours.
John Isner beat Nicolas Mahut at Wimbledon in 2010 over three days. The final set ended 70 to 68.
A cricket ball has six rows of stitches holding its leather together.
Fast bowlers use the raised seam to make the ball swing or bounce off in a new direction.
Football's offside rule is older than the crossbar.
Offside existed in early rules from the 1860s, while goals were sometimes just two posts with tape between them.
The first modern Olympics in 1896 had only 14 countries.
About 240 athletes, all men, competed in Athens. The 2024 Paris Games had more than 10,000 athletes.
Mount Everest climbers count as a sport too: Musa Ibrahim was the first Bangladeshi to the top.
He reached the summit in May 2010. Wasfia Nazreen later became the first Bangladeshi to climb the highest peak on every continent.
Siddikur Rahman was the first golfer from Bangladesh at the Olympics.
He played at the 2016 Rio Games, where golf returned to the Olympics after more than 100 years.
The Olympic flame is lit using the Sun.
At Olympia in Greece, a curved mirror focuses sunlight to light the torch, which is then carried to the host city.
Football boots once had metal toe caps.
Early boots were heavy leather work boots. Light, low boots arrived after the 1950s.
The Dhaka derby between Abahani and Mohammedan once filled stadiums.
In the 1980s and 90s the rivalry was so big that whole neighbourhoods split between the two clubs' colours.
